blocks.text: Isaiah 13 announces judgment against Babylon. The LORD musters a host, describes a day of wrath that brings fear, cosmic darkness, violence, and the collapse of human pride, and names the Medes as the attacking force. Babylon, called the glory of kingdoms and the beauty of Chaldean pride, is finally pictured as desolate and uninhabited.

Royal 'day of the king' imagery helps explain the chapter's metaphor, but Isaiah presents the LORD himself as judge and deliverer. The expression gathers the chapter's images of mustering, battle, wrath, judgment, and the overturning of proud power into a single decisive act of divine rule.

The oracle speaks amid imperial pressure and responds to the aggression and moral order of the nations. Babylon is not treated as beyond judgment because it is powerful; the chapter's announcement places even a celebrated empire under the LORD's evaluation.

sections.title: Empires as instruments and accountable powers

blocks.text: Isaiah judges Judah, Israel, and foreign nations, portraying empires as instruments that are themselves accountable. The oracle against Babylon belongs to that wider pattern: political power may appear in the prophetic scene, but it remains subject to judgment rather than becoming the final measure of history.
